Events Decouple Side Effects

Why creating a ticket doesn't itself send an email, write a notification, or push a socket update.

Creating a ticket needs to trigger a lot: a confirmation email to the customer, an in-app notification for every agent, a live update if one happens to be online watching the dashboard. The obvious way to write that is directly inside the function that creates the ticket — call the mailer, write the notification row, push the socket event, all in one place. The obvious way is also the wrong one here: it means createTicket has to know about email, in-app notifications, and real-time delivery, and changing any one of those three means editing and re-testing the function that actually creates tickets.

This project separates the two concerns instead, using domain events:

// Figure 0.3: the domain event names, one per moment something happens
export const EVENTS = {
  TICKET_CREATED: 'ticket.created',
  TICKET_ASSIGNED: 'ticket.assigned',
  TICKET_COMMENTED: 'ticket.commented',
  TICKET_STATUS_CHANGED: 'ticket.status_changed',
};

A service does its actual job — create the ticket, save it — and then announces that it happened, using Node's built-in EventEmitter (node:events; no extra dependency). It doesn't know or care who, if anyone, is listening. Separately, three listener modules each subscribe to the events they care about and react independently: one sends email (nodemailer), one writes the in-app Notification row, one pushes a live update over Socket.IO. Removing, breaking, or rewriting any one listener never touches the service that fired the event, or either of the other two listeners.

One more event exists beyond the four above, and it's different from the rest: a scheduled scan for tickets that have breached their SLA, which nothing in a request triggers — the next topic covers why that one needs a different mechanism entirely to run at all.
